name: Makeup sponge (beauty blender)

lead: A makeup sponge is a reusable foam tool, usually egg-shaped and edgeless, used to press and blend liquid, cream and powder makeup onto skin. The Beautyblender, introduced in the early 2000s, made the form widely popular.
It helps looks by making base makeup look smoother and less patchy, which evens out the appearance of skin tone and blemishes.

paras: Users dampen the sponge so it expands, then bounce or dab product onto the face rather than swiping. The pointed tip reaches around the eyes and nose. Sponges are washed between uses and replaced periodically.

Wet sponges can harbor bacteria if not cleaned and dried, so makeup guides recommend washing and not sharing them. Latex-free polyurethane foam is generally used, which suits people with latex sensitivity.

angle.text: The sponge changes how foundation sits on skin: dabbing a damp sponge blends product evenly, which people use to hide blemishes and uneven tone.

lead: A makeup sponge is a porous cosmetic applicator for blending foundation, concealer and similar products. Modern versions are made of hydrophilic polyurethane foam, shaped like an egg with a rounded base and pointed tip, and used damp [1].

According to Grokipedia, the design was developed by Hollywood makeup artist Rea Ann Silva around 2002 while working on a high-definition television show, where skin flaws were more visible; she rounded the edges of a triangular sponge to avoid lines and incorporated Beautyblender in 2003 [1]. Earlier sponges were wedge-shaped latex pieces, such as those that accompanied Max Factor's Pan-Cake foundation in the 1930s [1].

The appearance effect is a more even, airbrushed-looking base. Many brands now sell comparable sponges at lower prices, along with microfiber-covered and plant-based variants [1]. No clinical studies of makeup sponges were found.

paras: Typical sponges are egg- or teardrop-shaped, latex-free, washable and reusable [1]. Variants include flat wedges, microfiber-covered hybrids and sponges made partly from plant-based foam, such as Beautyblender's 2021 Bio Pure line [1].

Disposable latex wedges were professional kit standards through the late twentieth century, but their absorbency and edges made blending harder [1]. Silva's edgeless design and the practice of wetting the sponge spread from set work to retail, and the product is reported to have sold more than 50 million units by 2021 and to be in the Smithsonian collection [1]. These figures come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and are not independently confirmed here.
Standard cosmetic hygiene applies: wash sponges regularly and let them dry.
